column5: writing and recitation of Moses' memorial
column6: God tells Moses to write the Amalek memory in a book and rehearse it to Joshua. It concretely joins the commentary's Mosaic sheets to revealed words preserved by oral recitation.

column5: Book of the Covenant read aloud
column6: Moses takes a written covenant book and reads it to Israel; it supplies the page-to-hearing movement developed in the commentary.

column5: Moses finishes writing Torah in a book
column6: Within Deuteronomy Moses completes a written law-book. It is the closest Hebrew Bible anchor for the commentary's naming of Mosaic sheets, without equating their contents.
The book is deposited beside the ark as a witness against a resistant people; this sharpens 87:18's appeal to old writing against present objection.

column5: tablet and scroll for future days
column6: Isaiah's contested warning is deliberately written on tablet and scroll for future time. Its context explains why an insistently spoken warning can invoke an enduring document.
Habakkuk requires a vision to be legible to a reader on tablets, a material counterpart to the commentary's spread-out, visible sheets.
The written vision awaits an appointed end and will prove true; it supplies a Jewish-scriptural analogue for the commentary's ta'wil as a word's eventual arrival.

column5: fading grass and enduring divine word
column6: Isaiah contrasts perishing vegetation with God's word standing forever, matching the commentary's inference that an enduring word outlasts the near world.
Hilkiah's recovery of a long-neglected law book makes an old written word newly heard in Judah, a concrete alternative to calling its demand a novelty.
After the king burns Jeremiah's roll, a new scroll is ordered with all former words. It makes textual survival amid rejection a precise counterpart to old pages still speaking.
Torah is said to be near in mouth and heart for doing, not merely on an external object; this parallels the commentary's move from pages to memorized recitation.
Jeremiah relocates Torah from document to inward writing, a close Jewish analogue to the commentary's pages reappearing in a hearer's chest and voice.

column5: Ezekiel eats a scroll then speaks
column6: Ezekiel receives and consumes a physical scroll before speaking. Against the commentary's claim that the Qur'anic messenger is given recitation rather than a sheet, the contrast marks two modes of prophetic embodiment.

column5: book of remembrance, fear, and name
column6: The book records those who fear the Lord and esteem his name. It combines the commentary's unforgetting divine book with fear, name-remembrance, and worship.
God says the individual sinner will be blotted from his book, combining the commentary's divine record with its former-scroll rule of non-transferable guilt.
Mosaic law forbids executing children or parents for one another's sin. It is a direct legal antecedent to the commentary's 'no bearer bears another burden.'

column5: neither son nor father bears guilt
column6: Ezekiel states the same rule as a theological axiom, making the commentary's individual purification and accountability legible within a later Jewish prophetic debate.
Job's speaker says God returns a person's work to them; it corresponds precisely to the former-sheet sequence of effort seen and recompensed.
Daniel's throne vision opens books in the final court. It pairs the commentary's preserved book with an eschatological disclosure of human history.
Daniel raises the dead to everlasting life or abhorrence, giving explicit Hebrew Bible form to the commentary's insistence that the later life is the decisive enduring horizon.
Ecclesiastes describes dust returning to earth and spirit returning to God, a concise counterpart to the commentary's 'the destination is to the Lord.'
Jesus opposes gaining the whole world to losing one's life; this specifies the commentary's warning about preferring the near life over the better future.
Jesus tells hearers to work for food that endures into eternal life, a close formal parallel to near, perishing provision versus a lasting destination.
1 John explicitly contrasts the passing world and desire with the one doing God's will abiding forever, directly mirroring the temporal and enduring antithesis.
Paul says each person will bear their own load, an especially close Christian parallel to the commentary's no-vicarious-burden formulation.
Each worker receives a reward according to their own labor; this matches the commentary's link between personal striving and its later recompense.

column5: judgment according to deeds in body
column6: Each person appears before Christ's tribunal to receive what was done in the body, joining individual agency to the final outcome stressed by the commentary.

column5: opened books and judgment by deeds
column6: Revelation's dead are judged from opened books according to deeds. It makes the commentary's pages, personal effort, and final accounting one scene.

column5: wash yourselves and make yourselves clean
column6: Isaiah uses reflexive cleansing commands before ethical reform. That makes a concrete Hebrew parallel to 87:14's self-purification rather than a generic purity theme.
1 John links self-purification to hope in the appearing to come, closely joining the commentary's tazakka and its future horizon.
Raphael commends prayer together with fasting, almsgiving, and righteousness. It gives a Jewish late-antique counterpart to the commentary's prayer-and-purification pair.

column5: almsgiving purges sin and saves from death
column6: Tobit gives almsgiving an explicitly purgative and life-preserving effect, a precise Jewish comparison for purification expressed through giving.
Cornelius's prayers and alms rise as a memorial before God, directly pairing worship and giving like the commentary's surrounding prayer and purification.

column5: calling on the divine name and deliverance
column6: Hebrew Joel says everyone calling on YHWH's name will escape. It provides a direct older-scriptural counterpart to remembering the Lord's name and praying.
Pharaoh refuses Moses after asking who YHWH is. This is the closest Hebrew Bible scene to the commentary's Pharaoh asking Moses about his Lord.
Paul expressly says earlier writings were written for current instruction and hope, a Christian account of how an ancient corpus can address present hearers.
Jesus frames his mission as fulfillment rather than abolition of Law and Prophets. It is a Christian model of a later proclamation claiming continuity with earlier writings.
Jesus appeals to Moses's writing as testimony about him. The verse is a focused Christian rereading of Mosaic text as witness to a later message.
Luke groups Moses, Prophets, and Psalms as writings whose contents must be fulfilled. It gives a canonical Christian version of old scripture carrying a later realization.
Paul calls God's promise to Abraham a prior proclamation of the gospel. This is a particularly direct Christian expansion of the commentary's appeal to Abraham's earlier sheets.

column5: better heavenly country of the patriarchs
column6: Hebrews identifies the patriarchs' desired country as better and heavenly, placing Abraham's line inside the commentary's better, enduring-afterlife contrast.

column5: Moses rejects Egypt's treasure for reward
column6: Hebrews interprets Moses as valuing God's reproach above Egypt's treasures because he looked to reward. It supplies a Christian Mosaic reading of worldly preference versus future recompense.

column5: Moses and Prophets versus a demanded sign
column6: Abraham says those who do not hear Moses and the Prophets will not be persuaded even by resurrection. It closely matches the commentary's claim that a further visible sign or sheet would not cure refusal.

column5: examining Scripture to test a spoken message
column6: The Bereans test a newly preached word against the Scriptures daily. It gives a concrete reception practice for the commentary's assertion that a current utterance belongs with old writings.
Moses is publicly read in synagogues every Sabbath, showing how an ancient Mosaic text remains a voiced communal teaching rather than a mute archive.
Jesus receives, unrolls, and reads Isaiah's scroll in synagogue. The scene materializes the commentary's sheet, voice, and present hearer in one act.
Paul contrasts ink and stone with a Spirit-written letter on human hearts. This develops the same page-to-interior movement that the commentary draws from recitation.

column5: in the scroll of the book it is written of me
column6: Hebrews places its Christological claim in a book-scroll formula, a deliberate Christian claim that a later vocation is already inscribed in earlier Scripture.

column5: Moses offers blotting from the book for Israel
column6: Moses offers his own erasure from God's book for Israel's sin. In contrast to the commentary's non-transferable burden, it foregrounds intercession; the next verse returns judgment to each sinner.

Paul commands bearing one another's burdens. Against Galatians 6:5's individual load and the commentary's judicial rule, this preserves a social-ethical sense of shared burden rather than transferred guilt.
Ezekiel promises God will sprinkle clean water and cleanse Israel. This is a deliberate counterweight to the commentary's reflexive tazakka, locating cleansing chiefly in divine action.

column5: new covenant with Israel and Judah
column6: Jeremiah explicitly announces a new covenant with Israel and Judah. Alongside 87:18's denial that teaching is a mere novelty, it offers a different scriptural account in which newness and continuity coexist.

column5: a prophet charged with speaking falsehood
column6: Judean leaders tell Jeremiah he is speaking falsely. The concrete charge against a prophet's command parallels the commentary's anticipated claim that a revelation is the speaker's invention.
Jesus's hearers ask how he has learning without formal study. It gives a Christian analogue to the commentary's attention to a messenger who has not learned ancient pages by ordinary reading.

Hebrew aḥarit, 'end' or 'latter outcome,' is a cognate of the commentary's Arabic akhira. Isaiah's God declares the aḥarit from the beginning, a lexical and structural companion to first pages carrying their end.

column5: grass for cattle and plants for human use
column6: God causes grass for cattle and vegetation for human use. It closely matches the Taha–A'la comparison in the commentary: rain-grown plants, grazing animals, and provision after creation.
Jesus says all in tombs will hear his voice. It supplies a Christian answer to the commentary's question about the first generations: they too are gathered for a future day.

The Talmud debates whether Torah was given scroll by scroll or as a completed whole. That reception history directly illuminates the commentary's insistence that suhuf are discrete sheets rather than a bound codex.

Mishnah Avot presents Moses handing Torah through Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly. It makes the commentary's image of first writing leading later hearers into an explicit Jewish chain.

Rabbinic tradition says Abraham kept the whole Torah, even an eruv tavshilin. It offers a Jewish interpretive way to imagine Abraham as bearer of pre-Mosaic teaching, without positing extant Abrahamic pages.
Ezra says the law has been burned so no one knows what God has done or will do. It gives a Jewish counter-history to the commentary's confidence that former pages remain available.
After dictation restores books, Ezra is told to publish the first twenty-four for all readers. This furnishes a Jewish analogue to old written teaching made public again.

column5: seventy books reserved for the wise
column6: Ezra is told to reserve seventy books for the wise. This contrasts with the commentary's rhetorical picture of an openly sufficient earlier warning, while concretely extending its concern with pages hidden or disclosed.

column5: Old and New Testaments mutually disclose
column6: Augustine's formula that the New lies hidden in the Old and the Old becomes manifest in the New formalizes a Christian reading of the continuity claim, without making the Qur'anic text its premise.
Wisdom gives the righteous, though punished in human sight, a hope full of immortality. It is a Hellenistic Jewish articulation of the enduring future that the commentary sets over the near life.
